```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(simFastBOIN)
```

## The design

When two drugs are given together, the doses form a matrix, with the levels of
drug A in the rows and those of drug B in the columns. Toxicity increases along
every row and every column, but two combinations such as A3B1 (level 3 of drug
A with level 1 of drug B) and A1B3 cannot be ordered in advance, so the next
cohort may go in more than one direction. The
BOIN drug-combination design of Lin and Yin (2017) keeps the decision rule of
the single-agent design and adds a rule for the direction.

After each cohort, the observed DLT rate at the current combination is compared
with the boundaries `lambda_e` and `lambda_d` of the single-agent design. When
it calls for escalation, the next cohort goes one level up of drug A or of drug
B; when it calls for de-escalation, one level down. Between the two candidates
the design takes the one more likely to be near the target, the one with the
larger posterior probability that its DLT rate lies between `lambda_e` and
`lambda_d`. A combination judged too toxic is eliminated together
with every combination that has at least the same level of both drugs, and the
trial stops when the lowest combination is eliminated. At the end, the DLT rates
are smoothed by bivariate isotonic regression, so that they increase along every
row and column, and the combination closest to the target is the MTD.

The package follows the implementation in the BOIN package,
`BOIN::get.oc.comb()` with `mtd.contour = FALSE`, so that the two can be
compared trial by trial. That implementation adds a few details to the article:
a candidate's posterior probability is increased by 0.0005 for every patient
already treated there, so that ties go to the better informed combination; the
trial can stop at `n_earlystop`; and the MTD is selected from the estimates
`(y + 0.05) / (n + 0.1)`, with ties broken in favor of lower combinations.

## An example

The example of Yan et al. (2020) has three levels of drug A, four of drug B and
a target DLT rate of 0.25. Two combinations, A2B2 and A3B1, have a true DLT
rate of exactly 0.25.

```{r}
p_true <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.14,
                   0.08, 0.25, 0.42, 0.48,
                   0.25, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

oc <- sim_comb_boin(
  target = 0.25,
  p_true = p_true,
  n_cohort = 16,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_earlystop = 100,
  n_trials = 1000,
  seed = 6
)
oc
```

These are the settings of the article: 16 cohorts of three, early stopping
switched off with `n_earlystop = 100`, 1,000 trials and the seed 6, which is the
default of `BOIN::get.oc.comb()`. One of the two MTD combinations is selected in
`r round(oc$pct_true_mtd_selected, 1)`% of the trials, and
`r round(oc$pct_patients_true_mtd, 1)`% of the patients are treated at one of
them, the figures printed in the article. The package's tests check every
number of that output to the printed precision. The average number of patients
at A2B4 is exactly 1.905, half-way between two printed values, and the article
prints it as 1.90 whereas R 4.6.0 prints 1.91; how such a value is rounded
depends on the version of R.

The default `n_earlystop` of the package is 18, as for the single-agent design,
whereas `BOIN::get.oc.comb()` defaults to 100. Set it explicitly when comparing
the two.

## Comparing scenarios

`sim_comb_boin_multi()` runs the same design under several matrices of true DLT
rates and collects the main results in one row per scenario. Here are four of
the ten scenarios of Lin and Yin (2017), with three levels of agent 2 in the rows
and five of agent 1 in the columns, a target of 0.3 and 20 cohorts of three.

```{r}
scenarios <- list(
  "Scenario 1" = matrix(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45,
                          0.10, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.55,
                          0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.50, 0.60), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  "Scenario 4" = matrix(c(0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80,
                          0.45, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85,
                          0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  "Scenario 8" = matrix(c(0.02, 0.10, 0.15, 0.50, 0.60,
                          0.05, 0.12, 0.30, 0.55, 0.70,
                          0.08, 0.15, 0.45, 0.60, 0.80), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE),
  "Scenario 10" = matrix(c(0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45,
                           0.45, 0.50, 0.60, 0.65, 0.70,
                           0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85, 0.90), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
)

multi <- sim_comb_boin_multi(
  target = 0.30,
  scenarios = scenarios,
  n_cohort = 20,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_earlystop = 100,
  n_trials = 2000,
  seed = 123
)
multi
```

"True MTD" lists the combinations closest to the target, "MTD selected" the
percentage of trials that select one of them and "Patients at MTD" the
percentage of patients treated there. The full results of a scenario, with the
selection percentage of every combination, are an element of `multi$results`.

```{r}
multi$results[["Scenario 10"]]$sel_percent
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
stops_4 <- multi$results[["Scenario 4"]]$stop_reason_percent
eliminated_4 <- if ("lowest_dose_eliminated" %in% names(stops_4)) {
  stops_4[["lowest_dose_eliminated"]]
} else {
  0
}
```

In scenario 4 the lowest combination is itself the MTD, and
`r round(eliminated_4, 1)`% of the trials stop because it is eliminated. The script
`inst/validation/compare-with-LinYin2017.R` compares these and the other
scenarios with the tables of the article.

## Design options

The options of the single-agent design carry over: `titration` treats one
patient per combination, moving up one level of either drug at random, until the
first DLT; `extrasafe` adds a stricter stopping rule at the lowest combination;
`bound_mtd` refuses an MTD whose estimate reaches the de-escalation boundary;
and `start_dose` gives the levels of the two drugs for the first cohort.

With titration, the patients treated before the first DLT come on top of the
planned cohorts, as in the BOIN package: the first full cohort only tops up the
combination that titration reached.

## Working with the trial data

`comb_boin_simulate()` returns the trials themselves, as arrays with one row
per trial, and `comb_boin_select_mtd()` applies the selection rule to completed
trials, or to the data of a single trial given as two matrices.

```{r}
trials <- comb_boin_simulate(
  target = 0.25, p_true = p_true, n_cohort = 16, cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 5, seed = 1
)
trials$n_pts[1, , ]
trials$n_tox[1, , ]

comb_boin_select_mtd(trials$n_pts[1, , ], trials$n_tox[1, , ], target = 0.25)
```

The bivariate isotonic regression is computed by `Iso::biviso()`, the routine
that the BOIN package calls. This matters more than one might expect.
Combinations that the regression pools have equal estimates in exact arithmetic,
but not always in the last digits, and these digits decide between two
combinations on the same anti-diagonal. Another algorithm for the same
regression selects a different combination in a few trials out of a thousand.

## Agreement with the BOIN package

The engine draws one uniform variate per patient, in enrollment order, one for
the direction of every titration step that can go either way, and one for every
escalation or de-escalation that has a candidate. This is the order of
`BOIN::get.oc.comb()`, so with the same seed and matching arguments the two
implementations produce the same trials. The tests check this for several
settings whenever the BOIN package is installed, and
`inst/validation/compare-comb-with-BOIN.R` runs the comparison over a wider
grid.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
reference <- BOIN::get.oc.comb(
  target = 0.25, p.true = p_true, ncohort = 16, cohortsize = 3,
  n.earlystop = 18, ntrial = 1000, seed = 6
)

ours <- sim_comb_boin(
  target = 0.25, p_true = p_true, n_cohort = 16, cohort_size = 3,
  n_earlystop = 18, n_trials = 1000, seed = 6
)

all.equal(round(unname(ours$sel_percent), 2), unname(reference$selpercent))
all.equal(round(unname(ours$n_pts_dose), 2), unname(reference$npatients))
```

The waterfall design of Zhang and Yuan (2016), which searches for the whole MTD
contour rather than a single MTD, is not provided.

## References

Lin, R. and Yin, G. (2017). Bayesian Optimal Interval Design for Dose Finding in
Drug-Combination Trials. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research*, 26(5),
2155-2167.

Yan, F., Zhang, L., Zhou, Y., Pan, H., Liu, S. and Yuan, Y. (2020). BOIN: An R
Package for Designing Single-Agent and Drug-Combination Dose-Finding Trials Using
Bayesian Optimal Interval Designs. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 94(13),
1-32.

Zhang, L. and Yuan, Y. (2016). A Practical Bayesian Design to Identify the
Maximum Tolerated Dose Contour for Drug Combination Trials. *Statistics in
Medicine*, 35(27), 4924-4936.
